summary: With the World Cup packed up, intown Atlanta gets back to the everyday business of building, eating, and arguing over its streets. The city broke ground on an $18.5 million Monroe Drive Safe Streets redesign a decade in the making, while Invest Atlanta and the BeltLine rolled out up to $30,000 in down payment help for longtime residents on the south and west sides. Buckhead says a temporary goodbye to Apt 4B, Little Five Points lines up more tacos, and Amy Sherald's acclaimed 'American Sublime' hangs at the High Museum through September. In Summerhill, neighbors are fighting to keep the 1996 Olympic cauldron right where it belongs. Mayor Andre Dickens, meanwhile, took a victory lap on six weeks of World Cup festivities that turned Downtown into the center of the soccer world.

topStory.headline: Atlanta Breaks Ground on a Safer Monroe Drive After a Decade of Pushing
topStory.summary: The city broke ground on an $18.5 million redesign of Monroe Drive that trades a lane of traffic for a center turn lane and safer crossings, a project a decade in the making.
topStory.body: Monroe Drive is finally getting the makeover safety advocates have chased for ten years. On July 22, city officials broke ground on an $18.5 million Safe Streets project that will reshape the corridor from 8th Street to Piedmont Circle, according to SaportaReport. The plan converts Monroe Drive from four travel lanes to three: one lane in each direction plus a center turn lane, a design meant to calm the speeding that has long plagued the road on the edge of Midtown and Virginia-Highland. District 6 Councilmember Alex Wan put the goal plainly at the groundbreaking: slow traffic down. Monroe Drive sits on Atlanta's High Injury Network, the small share of roads that account for most of the city's serious crashes. The redesign grew out of years of community meetings and advocacy from groups like Atlanta Families for Safe Streets, who pushed for continuous bike lanes, better sidewalks, and crossings people can actually trust. The work is expected to take about two years. When it wraps, one of intown's busiest cut-throughs should be a calmer place to drive, bike, and walk.
topStory.imageAlt: Traffic moves along Monroe Drive in Atlanta ahead of the Safe Streets redesign

stories.headline: BeltLine and Invest Atlanta Launch Up to $30,000 in Down Payment Help
stories.summary: Invest Atlanta and Atlanta BeltLine launched a program offering up to $30,000 in down payment help for legacy residents and public workers buying in BeltLine neighborhoods.
stories.body: Buying a home along the BeltLine just got a little more reachable for the people who have lived alongside it the longest. Invest Atlanta and Atlanta BeltLine, Inc. have launched a down payment assistance program aimed at legacy residents and public sector employees, according to Rough Draft Atlanta. Eligible long-term residents and public servants (think teachers, first responders, and city workers) can receive up to $30,000 in assistance. Other qualified buyers may get up to $20,000. The money can go toward down payments, closing costs, an interest rate buydown, or principal reduction. The program covers homes inside the BeltLine Tax Allocation District on the south and west sides, the stretch that runs through neighborhoods like West End and Peoplestown. Buyers need a minimum credit score of 620, a household income at or below 140% of area median, and completion of a HUD-approved homebuyer course. Funding comes from the BeltLine's affordable housing budget and is administered by Invest Atlanta. For a corridor where rising prices have pushed out plenty of longtime residents, it is a real attempt to help some of them stay.
stories.imageAlt: A BeltLine trail scene in Atlanta where new down payment assistance applies

stories.headline: After the World Cup, South Downtown's Never-Built Towers Get a Second Look
stories.summary: With the World Cup crowds gone, Urbanize revisits the twin-tower housing plan that once promised to remake South Downtown and asks what it will take to finally bring residents downtown.
stories.body: Now that the World Cup tents are down, a familiar question is back: why don't more people live in Downtown Atlanta? Urbanize Atlanta revisited the twin towers of South Downtown that were supposed to answer it, and never got built. Four years ago the Newport plan for South Downtown kicked up as much urbanist excitement as anything in the city, promising dense new residential in the blocks around Underground Atlanta. Since then, hiked interest rates and a wobbly post-pandemic financing climate have stalled large downtown housing again and again, from a MARTA-adjacent parking lot on Forsyth Street that drew zero developer bids to a proposed tower over Underground. The World Cup showed what a lively South Downtown can look like when the crowds show up. The harder trick, as Urbanize notes, is making that energy stick with people who actually live there, and that takes the kind of dense residential the towers promised. For a district that just spent six weeks as the center of the soccer world, the next chapter is less glamorous and more important: getting somebody to build the housing.
stories.imageAlt: Rendering of proposed South Downtown towers along South Broad Street

stories.headline: Taqueria Taquito Express Is Bringing Tacos and Pupusas to Little Five Points
stories.summary: The local mini-chain Taqueria Taquito Express is bringing tacos, tortas, and pupusas to a small space on McLendon Avenue in Little Five Points.
stories.body: Little Five Points is getting more tacos. Local brand Taqueria Taquito Express has filed permits for a new location at 1165 McLendon Ave. NE, according to What Now Atlanta. The permit covers renovations on a compact 350-square-foot building, so expect a tight, order-and-go kind of spot. The menu runs the full lineup: tacos, burritos, tortas, quesadillas, nachos, and pupusas. Owner Chris Murphy confirmed the location, which is listed as coming soon on the company's website. It joins a growing local footprint of a dozen or so Taquito Express spots around metro Atlanta, and it lands the brand squarely in one of the city's most walkable, character-heavy corners.
stories.imageAlt: Taqueria Taquito Express signage ahead of its Little Five Points opening

stories.headline: Apt 4B Closes Its Original Buckhead Home as the Intown Dining Map Shifts
stories.summary: Buckhead's beloved Apt 4B is closing its original location after six years, while Midtown institution Mary Mac's Tea Room is making a change, per The Atlanta Voice's latest dining roundup.
stories.body: The intown dining map keeps shifting. In its latest restaurant roundup, The Atlanta Voice flags a notable goodbye in Buckhead: the Afro-Caribbean favorite Apt 4B is closing its original Peachtree Road location after six years. The good news for fans is that it is a see-you-later, not a farewell. The owners say they are hunting for a new home for the concept, known for live DJs, a deep vinyl collection, and a room styled like an eclectic New York apartment. In the meantime, some of its signature dishes will land at sister spots J'ouvert Caribbean Kitchen and Station 11. The roundup also notes a change at Mary Mac's Tea Room, the Midtown Southern institution that has been serving fried chicken and pot likker since 1945. Atlanta's restaurant scene is in its usual state of flux, with openings and closings trading places by the month.
stories.imageAlt: A plated dish from an Atlanta restaurant featured in a dining roundup

stories.headline: Amy Sherald's 'American Sublime' Comes Home to the High Museum
stories.summary: Georgia native Amy Sherald's acclaimed 'American Sublime' has come home to the High Museum, featuring more than 50 works including her official portrait of Michelle Obama.
stories.body: One of the most talked-about shows in American art right now is a hometown homecoming. Georgia native Amy Sherald's exhibition 'American Sublime' is on view at the High Museum of Art in Midtown, according to Atlanta Magazine. The show gathers more than 50 works, including Sherald's renowned official portrait of former first lady Michelle Obama. Born in Columbus, Sherald cross-enrolled in an art class at Spelman College, switched from a premedicine track to painting, and went on to win the High's David C. Driskell Prize in 2018. 'American Sublime' debuted at SFMOMA in 2024 and traveled to the Whitney and the Baltimore Museum of Art before arriving in Atlanta. It runs through September 27, which leaves plenty of summer to go see it. For a city that helped shape Sherald's early career, having the full show land at the High is a genuine moment.
stories.imageAlt: A painting from Amy Sherald's American Sublime exhibition at the High Museum

stories.headline: Summerhill Neighbors Push to Keep the 1996 Olympic Cauldron
stories.summary: Neighbors in Summerhill are pressing to keep the 1996 Olympic cauldron in the neighborhood, thirty years after the Games remade the area around the old Olympic stadium.
stories.body: Thirty years after the torch arrived, the 1996 Olympic cauldron is at the center of a neighborhood conversation in Summerhill. Residents are applying fresh pressure to keep the cauldron in the neighborhood where it has stood since the Games, according to Axios Atlanta. The cauldron tower sits near the site of the former Centennial Olympic Stadium, the venue that later became Turner Field and now anchors Georgia State's football program and the redevelopment reshaping the neighborhood. For an area that carried much of the Olympics' footprint, the cauldron is a rare physical reminder of that summer. The push comes as Atlanta marks three decades since the 1996 Games, a milestone the city has been revisiting all summer. Summerhill neighbors would like the next thirty years of that story to stay right where it started.
stories.imageAlt: The 1996 Olympic cauldron tower in Summerhill, Atlanta

stories.headline: Dickens Takes a Victory Lap as Atlanta Closes the Books on Its World Cup
stories.summary: Mayor Andre Dickens and city leaders gathered at City Hall to close out six weeks of World Cup festivities, calling the run proof Atlanta can host the world.
stories.body: The tents are down and the scorecards are in. Mayor Andre Dickens and city leaders gathered at City Hall to mark the end of six weeks of World Cup festivities, according to Fox 5 Atlanta. Hundreds of thousands of fans poured into Downtown between June 11 and July 19 for matches at Mercedes-Benz Stadium and 16 nights of fan festival. City officials pointed to the smooth logistics as proof the region can pull off an event of that scale. "We made a conscious decision that this event was going to happen with Atlanta and not to Atlanta," Dickens said, adding that "Atlanta is a group project" that no single person or agency could have carried alone. With the World Cup behind it, the city now turns to the harder question of what to keep: the transit habits, the downtown foot traffic, and the momentum that six weeks in the global spotlight can leave behind.
stories.imageAlt: Mayor Andre Dickens speaks at Atlanta City Hall about the World Cup
